audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant penultimate, not strict) rests on the standard reference grammar (Johnston 1980, PL B-70, 310 pp.) with a phonology appendix; both quoted sentences were confirmed verbatim in the now-saved open PDF (pp.256 and 180), and the grammar's own listed exceptions (enclitic deictics, intensifier -o, a handful of final-stressed words) justify 'dominant' rather than 'strict'. Glottolog lists no other grammar or phonology for naka1262, and the only later substantial work found (Chowning & Goodenough 2016 dictionary, downloaded) is silent on stress placement. Only housekeeping: the locator should read 'sect. 6.3 p.180 and App. A4 p.256' rather than '3.1.2, A4', and the record could note Johnston's remark that the penult nucleus is cued by pitch with intensity word-initial (A4.1.1).

sources.citation: Johnston 1980, Nakanai of New Britain, Pacific Linguistics B-70 — full PDF re-read from sealang.net (sects 3.1.2, A4)
sources.quote: The phonological word in Nakanai is a rhythmic segment with nuclear stress on the penultimate syllable, and bounded by juncture. [...] Stress consists mainly of increased intensity on the penultimate syllable of each separate word.

sources.quote: 'The phonological word in Nakanai is a rhythmic segment with nuclear stress on the penultimate syllable, and bounded by juncture.' (p.256); 'Stress consists mainly of increased intensity on the penultimate syllable of each separate word.' (p.180); exceptions: stress static with intensifier -o, static or final with deictics -e/-o, a few final-stressed words (tio, io, isa) (pp.257-258); 'The distinguishing characteristic of the nuclear syllable is primary pitch. Primary intensity occurs on the first syllable.' (A4.1.1, p.256).

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann & Ward H. Goodenough. 2016. A dictionary of the Lakalai (Nakanai) language of New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 29. Canberra: ANU. 421 pp. (open, hdl.handle.net/1885/107217)

sources.quote: No explicit stress-placement rule; only stress-conditioned processes ('Vowels are usually lengthened slightly when stressed'; /au/ > /o/ 'if the immediately following syllable has primary stress'; vowel drop in CVCV when 'stress falls on the second of the two vowels', e.g. alalavi > allavi). One lexical note: interrogative particle ia 'stressed on last syllable'.
